subsection: 1. The atmosphere and oceans as linked systems

notes.h: Linked exchanges between atmosphere and ocean
notes.b: The atmosphere (the envelope of gases around the earth) and the oceans are not separate. They swap heat, water, gases and momentum (movement), so a change in one alters the other.
points: Heat: the ocean warms or cools the air above it, depending on whether the sea surface is warmer or colder than the air.
Water: evaporation (liquid water turning to vapour) from the sea supplies the moisture for precipitation (rain, snow and so on) over both sea and land.
Gases: the ocean absorbs and releases carbon dioxide and oxygen, so it takes part in the air's chemistry as well as its weather.
Momentum: wind drives surface ocean currents, and the currents in turn shift the pressure and wind patterns above them, so the push goes both ways.

El Niño shows the link at work: a change in sea surface temperature across the Pacific alters atmospheric circulation (the large-scale pattern of air movement) there. There is more on this in Climatic environments and climate change.
notes.tip: If asked how the atmosphere and oceans are linked, give all four exchanges: heat, water, gases and momentum. Use El Niño as the example of a change in one altering the other.

notes.b: The ocean's effect on climate depends on how water handles heat. Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of a material, and water's is high.
points: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so the ocean heats and cools far more slowly than land and stores very large amounts of heat.
Because the ocean responds slowly, maritime climates (those near the sea) have small temperature ranges, the gap between the warmest and coldest readings.

The ocean has absorbed over 90% of the extra heat trapped by global warming, according to the IPCC (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the international body that assesses climate science). This shows how large its heat store is.
notes.tip: To explain small temperature ranges in maritime climates, give the reason: the ocean has a high specific heat capacity, so it heats and cools slowly.

notes.b: Air is a mixture of gases. The permanent gases are those whose share stays the same everywhere, and these figures are percentages by volume of dry air (air with the water vapour left out).
points: By volume, dry air is about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, so these two gases make up nearly all of it.
Argon makes up about 0.9% and carbon dioxide about 0.04%, so even the fourth gas is a tiny fraction.
Traces of neon, helium, methane, ozone and other gases make up the rest.
notes.tip: Learn the four figures and their order: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%.

notes.b: Some parts of the air change from place to place and time to time, unlike the permanent gases. These variable components matter far more than their small amounts suggest.
points: Water vapour (water as an invisible gas) ranges from almost 0% of the air over deserts and the poles to about 4% in hot, humid tropical air, because warm air can hold more of it.

Aerosols (tiny solid or liquid particles floating in the air), including dust, sea salt, smoke, volcanic ash and pollen, act as condensation nuclei, the surfaces on which water vapour condenses into droplets, and they scatter sunlight.
Ozone, a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule, is concentrated in the stratosphere, the layer of the atmosphere above the weather layer.
notes.tip: When asked for the variable components, list water vapour, aerosols and ozone, and give the range for water vapour (almost 0% to about 4%).

notes.b: Gases that make up only a tiny share of the air still control how much heat the earth keeps and how much harmful radiation reaches the ground.
points: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases: they absorb long-wave radiation (heat given off by the warm earth), which keeps the lower atmosphere warmer. There is more on this in Solar energy and its redistribution.
Ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, the high-energy part of sunlight that damages living tissue.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide was about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution and was over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s, because of human activity.
Carbon dioxide has been measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958. The record, known as the Keeling Curve, was begun by Charles David Keeling.
notes.tip: Remember that the ozone hole is not the cause of global warming. Greenhouse gases absorb long-wave radiation, while ozone absorbs ultraviolet.

notes.b: The air has weight, and gravity (the pull of the earth) keeps it from drifting off into space. This explains why the air gets thinner as you go up.
points: Gravity holds the atmosphere, so it is densest (most mass packed into a given space) at the surface and thins rapidly with height.
Pressure (the weight of the air pressing down) therefore falls with altitude, because less air lies above; about half the mass of the atmosphere lies below about 5.5 km.

notes.b: The atmosphere has four layers, separated by three pauses (boundaries between layers). Each layer is defined by how its temperature changes with height.
points: Diagram: draw a vertical profile with height in km on the vertical axis, label the four layers and the three pauses, and add the temperature line, which falls, rises, falls and rises again.
notes.tip: Temperature falls with height in the troposphere and mesosphere but rises in the stratosphere and thermosphere. Don't say it falls all the way up.

notes.b: The troposphere is the lowest layer and the one we live in. It is where weather happens.
points: It extends from the surface to about 8 km over the poles and about 16-18 km over the equator, being thicker where warm air expands and convection (warm air rising) is strongest.
Temperature falls with height at an average of about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m (the environmental lapse rate), because the air is heated from below by the ground.
It contains most of the atmosphere's mass and nearly all its water vapour, so nearly all weather and clouds occur here.
Its top is the tropopause, where the temperature stops falling; jet streams (fast, narrow bands of high-altitude wind) blow near it.
notes.tip: The troposphere is thicker over the equator than over the poles, not thinner. Give the reason: warm air expands and convection is strongest there.

notes.b: Above the tropopause the temperature trend reverses, because of the ozone layer, the stratosphere's special feature.
points: It extends from the tropopause to about 50 km.
Temperature rises with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and the absorbed energy warms the air; the ozone layer is concentrated at about 15-35 km.
It is very dry and stable, so few clouds form, but the anvils (flat, spread-out tops) of cumulonimbus clouds (tall storm clouds) spread out at its base.
Long-haul jets cruise near the tropopause to avoid turbulence (rough, bumpy air).
Its top is the stratopause.
notes.tip: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere, not the troposphere; ground-level ozone is a pollutant. Say that temperature rises here because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

notes.b: In the mesosphere, above the ozone layer's warming effect, temperature falls with height again.
points: It extends from about 50 km to about 80-85 km.
Temperature falls again with height, reaching about -90 °C at its top, the coldest point in the atmosphere.
Most meteors (rock fragments from space) burn up here. Its top is the mesopause.

notes.b: The outer layers are so thin that they behave very differently from the air near the ground.
points: Above about 85 km the air is very thin and its temperature rises sharply, because the few molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation; there are too few molecules for it to feel hot.
Auroras (northern lights, glowing displays in the sky) occur here, and the International Space Station orbits within it at about 400 km.
The exosphere is the outermost fringe, merging into space.
notes.tip: Temperature rises in the thermosphere because the few molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation. Add that it would not feel hot, as there are too few molecules.

notes.h: Extent and depth of the oceans
notes.b: Oceans dominate the planet's surface and its water, so they are the other half of the linked system.
points: The oceans cover about 71% of the earth's surface and hold about 97% of its water.
The five oceans are the Pacific (the largest and deepest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic; the Pacific covers about a third of the earth's surface.
Average ocean depth is about 3.7 km. The deepest point is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (a very deep, narrow trough in the sea floor), in the western Pacific, at about 11,000 m.

notes.b: Seawater is salty, and salinity is the measure of how salty. It is one of the main physical and chemical characteristics of the oceans.
points: Salinity is the dissolved salt content of seawater: about 35 parts per thousand on average, or 35 g of salt per kg.
Sodium chloride is the main salt, with magnesium, sulphate, calcium and potassium also present.
The salts come from rocks weathered (broken down) and carried by rivers and from volcanic gases and vents.

notes.b: Salinity is not the same everywhere. It rises where water is lost to the air and falls where fresh water is added.
points: Salinity is higher where evaporation exceeds precipitation, because water leaves but the salt stays behind, as in the subtropical oceans and in nearly enclosed seas in hot, dry areas.
The Red Sea, at about 40 parts per thousand, is among the saltiest open seas, and the Mediterranean is saltier than the Atlantic.
Salinity is lower where rainfall is heavy (the equatorial belt), where large rivers enter the sea and where ice melts (polar seas), because fresh water dilutes the salt.
The Baltic Sea is brackish (slightly salty), well under 10 parts per thousand in much of it, because of heavy river inflow and little evaporation.

When sea ice forms it leaves its salt behind, so the water beneath becomes saltier and denser; this feeds the thermohaline circulation (the deep ocean circulation driven by differences in temperature and salt). There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
notes.tip: Explain each variation by whether evaporation or fresh water (rain, rivers, melting ice) dominates. Don't add salinity figures of your own.

notes.b: The ocean is layered by temperature, just as the atmosphere is. The sun heats only the top, so the layers run from warm at the surface to cold below.
points: A warm, well-mixed surface layer, heated by the sun and stirred by wind, lies at the top of the tropical ocean, about the top 100-200 m.
The thermocline is the layer where temperature falls rapidly with depth.
The deep ocean is cold (about 0-4 °C) and dark, and is the largest part of the ocean by volume.
In polar waters there is little difference between the surface and the deep, so there is no strong thermocline.
Diagram: temperature against depth for a tropical ocean, showing the three layers.

notes.b: How dense seawater is decides whether it sinks or floats, and density depends on temperature and salinity.
points: Seawater is denser when it is colder and saltier; differences in density make water sink or rise and drive deep ocean circulation. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Surface temperature varies with latitude, from about 28-30 °C in the tropics to about -2 °C at the poles, which is the freezing point of seawater; ocean currents shift these patterns.

notes.b: The ocean also holds dissolved gases. Its uptake of carbon dioxide has a useful and a harmful effect.
points: The ocean dissolves oxygen, from the air and from phytoplankton (tiny floating plant-like organisms that give off oxygen), and carbon dioxide.
It has absorbed roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activity. This slows global warming but makes the water more acidic (ocean acidification), which harms corals and shellfish.
Average surface ocean pH (a scale measuring acidity, where lower means more acidic) has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times.
notes.tip: When asked about the ocean and carbon dioxide, give both sides: it slows global warming but causes ocean acidification, which harms corals and shellfish.

notes.b: To observe the atmosphere and oceans you need readings from many places at the same moment. Observing networks provide them.
points: Synoptic weather stations (stations that record the weather at the same moment as others), staffed or automatic, record at fixed times in UTC (a single world time standard) to World Meteorological Organization (WMO) standards, so that readings can be compared worldwide.
Other sources include ships, buoys, aircraft, weather balloons, radar and satellites.
Met Éireann (the Irish national weather service) collects the Irish data. There is more on this in Weather maps and weather data.
notes.tip: Exams ask both how things are measured and why it matters. For each phenomenon give the instrument, how it works, units and siting.

notes.b: Temperature is measured by several instruments, each suited to a different job, and a screen keeps the readings honest.
points: A liquid-in-glass thermometer uses mercury or alcohol, which expands and rises up a narrow tube as it warms.

A maximum-minimum thermometer, Six's thermometer, uses small metal indexes (markers) that are pushed up to the highest and lowest points reached and stay there until reset with a magnet; it is read once a day and then reset. James Six invented it in 1782.
Electronic thermometers in automatic stations use sensors whose electrical resistance changes with temperature; a thermograph gives a continuous trace.

Thermometers sit in a Stevenson screen (a ventilated white box) about 1.25 m above the ground. It is white to reflect sunlight, louvred (slatted) to let air circulate, and mounted on legs above grass.
The Stevenson screen's door faces away from direct sun (north in Ireland), so readings are true shade air temperatures.
A grass minimum thermometer, laid just above short grass, measures ground frost.
Daily mean, daily range and annual range are derived from these readings. There is more on the calculation method in Weather maps and weather data.
notes.tip: In Ireland the Stevenson screen door faces north, away from the sun. Give a reason for each feature of the screen.

notes.b: Air pressure is the weight of the air above, and two types of barometer measure it in different ways.
points: A mercury barometer: the weight of the atmosphere supports a column of mercury in a glass tube, and the column rises as pressure rises. Evangelista Torricelli invented it in 1643.

An aneroid barometer (aneroid means without liquid) uses a sealed, partly emptied metal capsule that is squeezed in as pressure rises and expands as it falls; levers move a needle on a dial. It is portable, so it is used in homes and on ships.
A barograph links an aneroid to a pen that draws a continuous record on a rotating drum; the trend of rising or falling pressure matters most in forecasting.
Electronic pressure sensors are used in automatic stations.

Readings are corrected to mean sea level so that stations at different heights can be compared and isobars (lines joining places of equal pressure) drawn. Pressure is measured in hPa (hectopascals, equal to mb), with an average of about 1013 hPa.
notes.tip: A barometer measures pressure, so don't swap it with the hygrometer (humidity) or anemometer (wind speed). Remember that aneroid means without liquid.

notes.b: Wind speed is measured by an anemometer, standing at a standard height so that readings can be compared.
points: A cup anemometer has three or four cups on arms that spin faster as wind speed rises; the turns are counted electrically and converted to speed.
Sonic anemometers, which have no moving parts, are used on some modern stations.
The WMO standard height for surface wind is 10 m above open ground, away from buildings and trees, which would shelter the instrument and lower its readings.
Speed is given in km/h, knots or m/s, and gusts (short bursts of stronger wind) are recorded separately from mean speed. Without instruments, speed is estimated using the Beaufort scale.

notes.b: Wind direction is the way the wind blows from, and it is shown by a vane or a windsock.
points: A wind vane has a large tail that is pushed downwind, so its pointer faces the direction the wind blows from; direction is read against compass points or degrees.
Windsocks show wind direction and strength at airports.
Wind is always named from the direction it comes from, so a westerly wind blows from the west.
notes.tip: A wind vane points into the wind, towards where it comes from. Don't give the direction it is blowing to.

notes.b: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. The wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer measures it by using evaporative cooling.
points: A wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer (psychrometer) has two thermometers side by side. The wet bulb is wrapped in muslin (thin cloth) kept wet from a water reservoir; evaporation from the muslin cools it, so it reads lower than the dry bulb.
The drier the air, the faster the evaporation and the bigger the difference, called the wet bulb depression. If both thermometers read the same, the air is saturated (holding all the vapour it can).
Relative humidity, given as a percentage, is read from tables using the dry bulb reading and the difference between the two readings.
A hair hygrometer uses human hair, which lengthens in humid air and shortens in dry air, to move a pointer.
Automatic stations use electronic (capacitance) sensors.
notes.tip: A large difference between the two thermometers means dry air, with low relative humidity; no difference means saturated air. If an example reading is needed, use an invented one such as dry bulb 15 °C, wet bulb 12 °C, a 3 °C difference.

notes.b: Rain, sunshine, evaporation and cloud each have their own instrument.
points: Rain gauge: a funnel of standard size, set in open ground with its rim raised above the surface to avoid splash, collects rain into a measuring cylinder that is read in mm each day; tipping-bucket gauges record automatically.
Campbell-Stokes sunshine recorder: a glass sphere focuses the sun's rays and burns a trace on a card; the length of the burn gives hours of bright sunshine.
Evaporation pan: measures the water lost from an open water surface by evaporation.
Cloud cover is estimated in oktas (eighths of the sky covered) by observers or measured by ceilometers (instruments that find the height of cloud bases).

notes.b: Weather also has to be measured high above the ground, where ground instruments cannot reach.
points: Weather balloons carry radiosondes, small instrument packs that measure temperature, humidity and pressure and radio them back; tracking the balloon gives the upper winds.

Balloons are launched twice a day, at fixed times, from stations worldwide, including Valentia Observatory, Co. Kerry, which has one of the longest weather records in Ireland, dating from the 19th century.
Aircraft also report temperature and wind automatically.

notes.b: Remote sensing means measuring from a distance, without touching the thing measured.
points: Geostationary (fixed over one spot) and polar-orbiting (passing over the poles) weather satellites measure cloud, sea-surface temperature, water vapour and ice. There is more on this in Satellite imagery.
Rainfall radar detects precipitation from the echo returned by raindrops.

notes.b: Ocean measurements come from instruments floating on, drifting in and orbiting above the sea. Together they supply the data on the ocean side of the linked system.
points: Moored weather buoys (anchored floating stations) record air pressure, air and sea temperature, wind, wave height and humidity, and transmit the readings, hourly. The Irish Marine Data Buoy Observation Network, run by the Marine Institute with Met Éireann, moors such buoys off the Irish coast.
Drifting buoys follow ocean currents, and voluntary observing ships report weather at sea.

Argo floats drift at depth, rise to the surface every 10 days or so, and measure temperature and salinity down to about 2,000 m before transmitting by satellite. The Argo programme began in 2000, and about 4,000 floats now drift in the world's oceans.
Tide gauges and satellite altimeters (instruments that measure height from space) measure sea level; satellites also measure sea-surface temperature and sea ice.
Research ships lower CTD instruments (conductivity, temperature, depth) to sample salinity and temperature at depth.
The TAO array, a line of moored buoys across the equatorial Pacific, monitors the ocean to give warning of El Niño.
notes.tip: For ocean measurement name the main tools: buoys, Argo floats and satellites. Say what each one measures.

notes.b: A reading is only useful if it is trustworthy, so how and where instruments are set up matters as much as the instrument.
points: Instruments must be correctly sited: in an open place, at the standard height, shaded for thermometers and away from buildings and heated surfaces, which would distort the readings.
Instruments must be regularly calibrated (checked against a standard), read at the same times each day, and long records kept at the same site, so the record stays consistent.
Urban growth around a station (the urban heat island, the extra warmth of built-up areas) can bias its records upward.

notes.b: Measurements are collected because they are used. Each use below is a separate reason, from forecasting and safety to farming, energy and climate science.
points: Forecasting: observations are the starting point (initial conditions) for computer forecast models, and more and better observations give better forecasts.
Warnings: storm, rain, snow and heat warnings, including Met Éireann's colour codes, save lives and property. There is more on this in Weather maps and weather data.

Storm surge (sea level raised by a storm) and flood warnings are issued, and tropical cyclones are tracked; a falling barograph trace warns of an approaching depression (a low-pressure weather system).

Aviation needs wind, visibility, icing and pressure for altimeter settings (so a plane's height reading is correct); shipping and fishing need sea area forecasts and wave heights from buoys; offshore work depends on the same data.

Farming: the timing of silage and hay making, spraying, sowing and harvesting depends on forecasts; frost warnings protect crops; soil temperature and moisture show when grass starts to grow; drought monitoring is also part of this use. There is more on drought in Climate and economic development.

Energy and the economy: wind measurements are used to site wind farms and predict their output; temperature forecasts predict electricity and gas demand; construction, retail, insurance, sport and tourism planning all use weather data.

Climate records: long, consistent records, such as the Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record and Valentia's long weather record, show trends including global warming, sea-level rise and ocean warming; they are the evidence used by the IPCC and by governments.
The IPCC was set up in 1988 by the WMO and the UN Environment Programme.
Ocean-atmosphere link: buoy and Argo data on sea temperature and salinity track El Niño, ocean heat content and the Atlantic circulation, and they improve seasonal forecasts.
notes.tip: Treat each use as a separate point: forecasting, warnings, aviation and shipping, farming, energy, and climate-change evidence. Examiners ask both how phenomena are measured and why the measurements matter.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of a unit mass of a substance by one degree; water's high value means the ocean heats and cools slowly.
The average rate at which air temperature falls with height in the troposphere, about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m.
The boundary at the top of the troposphere, where temperature stops falling with height.
The layer of the ocean where temperature falls rapidly with depth, between the warm surface layer and the cold deep ocean.
The amount of dissolved salt in seawater, measured in parts per thousand.
A pressure instrument with a sealed, partly emptied metal capsule that changes shape as pressure changes, moving a needle on a dial.
The difference between the dry bulb and wet bulb readings; the bigger it is, the drier the air.
A white, louvred shelter that holds thermometers in true shade air, with its door facing away from direct sun.
A small instrument pack carried by a weather balloon that measures temperature, humidity and pressure and radios the readings back.
A drifting instrument that rises and sinks in the ocean, measuring temperature and salinity to about 2,000 m and transmitting the data by satellite.

factCards.term: Atmosphere and oceans: the four things they exchange as one linked system
factCards.definition: Heat (the ocean warms or cools the air above it); water (evaporation and precipitation); gases (the ocean absorbs and releases carbon dioxide and oxygen); momentum (wind drives surface currents, and currents shift pressure and wind patterns).

factCards.term: Dry air: the four main gases and their share by volume
factCards.definition: Nitrogen about 78%; oxygen about 21%; argon about 0.9%; carbon dioxide about 0.04%. Traces of neon, helium, methane, ozone and other gases make up the rest.

factCards.term: Name three variable components of the atmosphere
factCards.definition: Water vapour, from almost 0% over deserts and the poles to about 4% in hot, humid tropical air; aerosols (dust, sea salt, smoke, volcanic ash, pollen) that act as condensation nuclei and scatter sunlight; ozone, concentrated in the stratosphere.

factCards.term: Atmospheric carbon dioxide: key figures and where it is measured
factCards.definition: About 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution and over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s, because of human activity. Measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958: the Keeling Curve, begun by Charles David Keeling.

factCards.term: Troposphere: height, temperature trend and why weather happens there
factCards.definition: Up to about 8 km over the poles and 16 to 18 km over the equator. Temperature falls with height because the air is heated from below by the ground. It holds most of the atmosphere's mass and nearly all its water vapour, so nearly all weather occurs here.

factCards.term: Stratosphere: height, temperature trend and key features
factCards.definition: From the tropopause to about 50 km. Temperature rises with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation; the ozone layer is at about 15 to 35 km. Very dry and stable, so few clouds form, but cumulonimbus anvils spread out at its base.

factCards.term: Mesosphere and thermosphere: temperature trend and one feature of each
factCards.definition: Mesosphere (about 50 to 80-85 km): temperature falls to about −90 °C, the coldest point; most meteors burn up here. Thermosphere (above about 85 km): temperature rises sharply as its few molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation; auroras occur here.

factCards.term: Oceans: key figures for extent and depth
factCards.definition: Cover about 71% of the earth's surface and hold about 97% of its water; average depth about 3.7 km. Deepest point: the Challenger Deep, Mariana Trench, western Pacific, about 11,000 m. The Pacific covers about a third of the earth's surface.

factCards.term: Seawater salinity: average figure and where the salts come from
factCards.definition: About 35 parts per thousand (35 g of salt per kg) on average, mostly sodium chloride, with magnesium, sulphate, calcium and potassium. The salts come from rocks weathered and carried by rivers and from volcanic gases and vents.

factCards.term: Salinity: why it varies, with named seas
factCards.definition: Higher where evaporation exceeds precipitation: subtropical oceans, the Red Sea (about 40 parts per thousand) and the Mediterranean. Lower where rain is heavy, large rivers enter or ice melts: the Baltic is brackish, well under 10 parts per thousand.

factCards.term: Ocean temperature layers: the three layers from the surface down
factCards.definition: A warm, well-mixed surface layer heated by the sun and stirred by wind; the thermocline, where temperature falls rapidly with depth; the cold (about 0 to 4 °C), dark deep ocean, the largest part by volume. Polar waters change little with depth.

factCards.term: Seawater density: what makes water sink and why it matters
factCards.definition: Water is denser when colder and saltier. When sea ice forms it leaves its salt behind, so the water beneath becomes saltier and denser and sinks; these density differences drive the deep ocean circulation.

factCards.term: The ocean as a store of heat and carbon: key figures and one effect
factCards.definition: It has taken up over 90% of the extra heat from global warming (IPCC) and roughly a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions. This slows warming but acidifies the water: surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1, harming corals and shellfish.

factCards.term: Measuring temperature: how three thermometers work
factCards.definition: Liquid-in-glass: mercury or alcohol expands up a narrow tube. Six's maximum-minimum (invented by James Six): metal indexes are pushed to the highest and lowest points, read daily and reset with a magnet. Electronic: a sensor's resistance changes with temperature.

factCards.term: Measuring pressure: mercury barometer, barograph and sea-level correction
factCards.definition: Mercury barometer (Torricelli, 1643): the atmosphere's weight holds up a mercury column that rises as pressure rises. Barograph: an aneroid drives a pen on a rotating drum, giving a continuous trace. Readings are corrected to mean sea level for comparison.

factCards.term: Wind: how speed and direction are measured and the standard height
factCards.definition: A cup anemometer's three or four cups spin faster as wind rises; turns are counted electrically and converted to speed. A wind vane's large tail is pushed downwind, so its pointer faces where the wind comes from. Standard height: 10 m above open ground.

factCards.term: Wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer: steps to find relative humidity
factCards.definition: Read the dry bulb; read the wet bulb, whose wet muslin is cooled by evaporation so it reads lower; subtract to get the difference; look up relative humidity in tables using the dry bulb reading and the difference. Equal readings mean saturated air.

factCards.term: Rain gauge and Campbell–Stokes sunshine recorder: how each works
factCards.definition: Rain gauge: a standard funnel, rim raised above open ground to avoid splash, drains into a measuring cylinder read in mm daily. Campbell–Stokes: a glass sphere focuses the sun's rays to burn a trace on a card; the burn length gives hours of sunshine.

factCards.term: Valentia Observatory, Co. Kerry: two reasons it matters
factCards.definition: It launches weather balloons carrying radiosondes, and tracking the balloons gives upper winds; it has one of the longest weather records in Ireland, from the 19th century, used to show climate trends.

factCards.term: Measuring the oceans: four methods besides Argo floats
factCards.definition: Moored buoys of the Irish Marine Data Buoy Observation Network (Marine Institute with Met Éireann) record pressure, temperature, wind and waves; drifting buoys follow currents; altimeters and tide gauges measure sea level; research ships lower CTD instruments.

factCards.term: Ocean data: how they help explain the ocean–atmosphere link
factCards.definition: Buoy and Argo data on sea temperature and salinity track El Niño, ocean heat content and the Atlantic circulation, improving seasonal forecasts; the TAO array of moored buoys across the equatorial Pacific gives warning of El Niño.

factCards.term: Weather records: four rules for accurate readings
factCards.definition: Site instruments correctly (open ground, standard height, thermometers shaded, away from buildings); calibrate them regularly; read them at the same times each day; keep long records at one site, as urban growth can bias readings upward.

factCards.term: Weather measurements: importance for forecasts and warnings
factCards.definition: Observations are the initial conditions for computer forecast models, so more and better data give better forecasts; they support storm, rain, snow, heat, storm-surge and flood warnings; a falling barograph trace warns of an approaching depression.

factCards.term: Weather measurements: four economic uses
factCards.definition: Aviation (wind, visibility, icing, altimeter settings); shipping and fishing (sea area forecasts, wave heights from buoys); farming (timing silage, spraying and harvesting, frost warnings); energy (siting wind farms, predicting electricity and gas demand).

factCards.term: Climate records: why long measurement records matter
factCards.definition: Long, consistent records such as Mauna Loa's carbon dioxide record and Valentia's weather record show global warming, sea-level rise and ocean warming; they are evidence for governments and the IPCC (set up in 1988 by the WMO and UN Environment Programme).

questions.prompt: Give an account of how atmosphere–ocean phenomena (pressure, temperature, wind and humidity) are measured and examine the importance of such measurements.
questions.model: Pressure: a mercury barometer, invented by Evangelista Torricelli in 1643, balances the weight of the atmosphere against a column of mercury; an aneroid barometer uses a sealed, partly emptied metal capsule linked to a dial; a barograph draws a continuous record. Readings are in hPa, corrected to mean sea level, with an average of about 1013 hPa, and are taken in open sites away from buildings. Temperature: liquid-in-glass and electronic thermometers, a maximum-minimum (Six's) thermometer and a grass minimum thermometer, all sheltered in a Stevenson screen about 1.25 m above grass with its door facing north in Ireland, so that readings are true shade air temperatures in degrees Celsius (°C). Wind: a cup anemometer whose turns are counted electrically gives speed, and a wind vane whose pointer faces the direction the wind blows from gives direction; both are sited at the WMO standard height of 10 m above open ground, with speed in km/h, knots or m/s and gusts recorded separately. Humidity: a wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer, where evaporation from the wet muslin cools the wet bulb, and the difference between the two readings is used with a table to find relative humidity as a percentage; a hair hygrometer and electronic sensors are alternatives. Importance: observations start computer forecasts, and warnings of storms, floods, heat and cold save lives and property; aviation, shipping and fishing need wind, visibility and wave data from buoys; farmers use frost, soil and drought information; energy planners use wind data for wind farms and temperature forecasts for electricity and gas demand. Over the oceans, moored buoys, drifting buoys, voluntary ships, Argo floats (about 4,000 floats measuring temperature and salinity to about 2,000 m), tide gauges, satellites and research ships with CTD instruments supply the data, and the TAO array gives warning of El Niño. Long, consistent records show global warming, sea-level rise and ocean warming, and provide the evidence the IPCC and governments use.

questions.prompt: The atmosphere and the oceans are linked systems with distinctive physical and chemical characteristics. Discuss.
questions.model: Composition: dry air is about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, with argon about 0.9% and carbon dioxide about 0.04%; water vapour varies from almost 0% to about 4%; aerosols act as condensation nuclei; ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere and absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Layers: the troposphere, up to about 8 km over the poles and 16–18 km over the equator, cools with height at about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m and holds nearly all the weather; the stratosphere, to about 50 km, warms with height because of ozone at about 15–35 km; the mesosphere, to about 80–85 km, cools to about −90 °C; the thermosphere above warms because its few molecules absorb solar radiation, and the International Space Station orbits in it at about 400 km. Oceans: salinity averages about 35 parts per thousand, mostly sodium chloride, and is higher where evaporation exceeds precipitation (the Red Sea at about 40 parts per thousand, the Mediterranean) and lower in the equatorial belt, at river mouths and in polar seas, while the Baltic is brackish. Temperature layers: a warm, mixed surface layer, a thermocline where temperature falls rapidly, and a cold deep ocean at about 0–4 °C that makes up most of its volume. Density: seawater is denser when colder and saltier, so cold, salty water sinks and drives deep circulation; surface temperature runs from about 28–30 °C in the tropics to about −2 °C, the freezing point of seawater, at the poles. Links: heat is exchanged, since the ocean has absorbed over 90% of the extra heat from global warming; water is exchanged through evaporation and precipitation; gases are exchanged, since the ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions, lowering surface pH from about 8.2 to about 8.1 and causing acidification; momentum is exchanged, since wind drives currents that shift pressure and wind patterns. El Niño shows the systems changing together.

questions.prompt: Explain how a wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer is used to find relative humidity.
questions.model: 1. Read the dry bulb thermometer, which records the true air temperature. 2. Read the wet bulb thermometer, whose bulb is wrapped in muslin kept wet from a water reservoir; evaporation from the muslin cools it, so it reads lower than the dry bulb. 3. Subtract the wet bulb reading from the dry bulb reading to find the wet bulb depression; the drier the air, the bigger the difference, and two equal readings mean saturated air. 4. Use the dry bulb reading and the difference in a humidity table to read the relative humidity as a percentage. Illustrative example: dry bulb 15 °C, wet bulb 12 °C, a 3 °C difference; the table converts this into a relative humidity well below 100%, showing the air is not saturated.
